paragraphs: Joseph Solman
(Unintelligible) Okay. So let me ask you, I have about 20 questions, and then if there's anything that you feel that we haven't gone over, we can...
Well, I'll expand on some of the questions, or I'll modify them, whatever. Okay.
Go ahead.

When did you first become acquainted with Maurice Sievan and his work? I first became acquainted with Maurice Sievan in the Federation of Modern Painters and Sculptors that we were both members of. My guess is somewhere in the mid or late 50s. No, not late 50s. I'm sorry. the late 40s or early 50s is when I first became acquainted with him. He was a member of a group. There must have been 60 or 70 members of that group. Was there a name for the group?
Yes, the Federation of Modern Painters and Sculptors, which still exists. Yes. And what kind of work was he doing then?
As I remember, he was doing the Flushing street scenes, the kind of expressionist, very loosely handled, semi-expressionist, semi-romantic street scenes.
And can you describe any of that work more specifically?
Well, I think I've described it in full detail in a preface to a catalog for a show he had in 1955 at the Mint College. The Mint Museum.
Mint Museum in North Carolina.

I think if you gave me the thing, I would take a paragraph after that because I spend a lot of time writing. I like writing, but it comes very hard to me. And since I worked very hard on it, rather than improvise, I'd sooner read a paragraph out of it. Okay. Just for the purpose of the video, try not to look at the camera. We'll just have a little conversation.
I'm not looking at the camera. I'm looking at you.
Okay, good. Now, what was Maurice Sievan like as a person?

Maurice Sievan was a loner, in my opinion, a strange mixture of a quiet sardonic humor, which always expressed itself in a kind of negative way about odder(?) people, or a rather curious individualistic way. it was hard to follow some of his meanings and statements. He could quote the Bible. I know he was a big biblical guy because he's quoted to me. And he thought very little of some of the painting modes of his time. I think by living, did he live in Flushing? Yeah.

by teaching and learning and flushing, he was a little isolated from the mainstream of art, not that he didn't even come in to see exhibitions and discuss them with all of us, but I feel that he was a little reclusive in a certain sense. And so he might not show up at meetings very often because he lived out there, but when he did show up, he was always with his wife, Leah (Lee). And my feeling is that he deepened his art of the neighborhood streets of Flushing away from the general category of art of that time. And therefore, I think he felt, if not isolated, at least separate from the general movements. I can't tell you why, but I don't think at the time I met him, he was making any great efforts to have one-man shows. In fact, I don't know of any. And when he, I had been doing some art criticism for a couple of magazines, which I gave up because I think an artist should not write art criticism. But he liked my viewpoint, apparently, and he asked me to look at his work and whether I would consider doing a preface for a catalog. I looked at his work, that's the first time I saw it in great abundance. And I was very impressed with his very local color and yet very modern expressionist feeling for those streets. I felt no one had done the poetry of the suburbs just like he had done. I was sympathetic because I was first recognized in the mid-30s and late-30s for my street scenes in New York,

the broken down east side street scenes, which I did in a much flatter, more semi-abstract way. And I achieved some recognition then. And then there was a formation of a group called The Ten in 1935 in my studio that included Rothko and Adolf Gottlieb and Ilya Baratowski and so on and so forth. So I was pretty well known by that time. But I liked his intimate, individual, personal interpretation of those little suburban streets. Because I was brought up in Jamaica, Long Island when I was a youth. And I first learned to do the alleys and streets of South Jamaica. So I felt a certain kinship and feeling for his work. And that's why I wrote the catalog, because I liked his work very much.

that's great, um, can you talk about kind of the personality of his landscapes i mean in doing a landscape uh everybody kind of puts a little bit of them themselves into it did he have a personality in his landscape?

Well he certainly did he uh when he did those the little uh one or two story houses in Flushing with the little cars parked outside and the trees and so on. He did them in such a rough and tumble style and yet there was a sense of intimacy and a knowledge of that neighborhood so well that, well, like any true artist, he was digging in to a visual subject that he was seeing every single day of his life. And that's why I liked it so much.
Do you have any personal anecdotes about Maurice Sievan?

Yes, a few. As I say, he wouldn't come to every meeting of the Federation. I'd meet him at galleries and so on. And I remember when I met him in the late 60s at some gallery or other, some publisher, crowd publishers, had produced a book on my work covering about 32 years of my work. And I had a show in conjunction with our book at the ACA Gallery. He saw it, he was there, and he told me, "Joe," he said "you've got a new renaissance." You know, he was very proud of me for the show and the book. And we got to talking about the general atmosphere of the art world around that period. And we spoke about the avant-garde, that means de Koenig, Pollock, Rothko, Franz Kline. and he told me then which surprised me that he had been visiting Mark Rothko at his studio now I had lost contact with Mark Rothko because our group dissolved around 1940 and he went his way and became abstracto he was figurative beforehand and he got in with Motherwell and Kline and I'm talking about Rothko. And I didn't know that Sievan, so I didn't see Mark Rothko, although I liked his work, but Maurice Sievan obviously was getting interested in the work of that genre. And he told me about his visits to Rothko and I can't remember exactly what he said, but he had become very friendly with him. Rothko was a strange loner also, so I think there was a personality kinship there. But apparently, that began to affect his work. I believe he felt, I think that Maurice felt he'd been out of the running. He hadn't had many shows. I rarely saw a show of his in New York. I did not see his shows at
Contemporary Arts in the 40s, because I'd had a show there back in 1934. So I met him really in the late 40s or 50s. But I feel, he lived in Provincetown , didn't he have a place in Provincetown?
Yeah, in the summers.

In the summers. And once when we were there in, I'm trying to remember when, I think it was in the 60s, mid-60s, to visit the widow of Byron Brown. She invited us for an eight-day stay because I was a very close friend with Byron Brown, who was an abstract and figurative painter. And I passed by to see Maurice Sievan, and he was beginning to paint black and gray canvases. And obviously he was influenced by, not necessarily by Rothko or Gottlieb or Franz Klien, But he apparently felt that his absorption in the Flushing streets and so on was sort of passé. Because the work, he was stretching larger canvases. He was working in almost two tones, black and gray or green and gray and green and black and so on. There was two 9might figurative?), he would call him Mr. Dash or Mr. This, or he'd make up some crazy name like PFF or something like that. And I realized that he was being influenced, which is perfectly natural, by this new dynamic movement of art in America. And I was a little disappointed. I didn't mean that any artist should stick to one mode all his life. Far from it, because I have changed four or five or six times in my life, and so have many artists. But I felt that he did not incorporate some of his early work into the new work. It was like a new tableau, a new shift, an entirely new shift. And I didn't express my disappointment because his gift of putting on paint was remarkable. He would slash in some blacks and grays in a lovely way. It almost looked like a Chinese triptych or something of the sort. And then later I saw a few of his things of that nature in some of our group shows of the Federation. We used to have one or two shows a year at some place that was hospitable enough to give us a show. And I think I was a little disappointed because, though it must have been Maurice Sievan's soul and his real thing, I felt he didn't pull along, like all artists do, the baggage of their earlier work into their new work. When you watch, when you look at the development of a Cezanne or a Pissarro, or even a chameleon great artists like Picasso, you notice that they drag along some of their earlier baggage in their work. And I didn't feel he was doing that, except for a kind of expressionist flourish. And that disappointed me a bit.
Yeah, yeah. His work did change pretty drastically.
Yeah.
Okay. That kind of leads me right into the next question, actually. How do you think Sievan fit
into the art scene of the time? And really, there were many times, but maybe you can discuss almost.

Well, my only feeling is that the work of the 40s and 50s that I wrote about when he had that Mint Museum show, I don't think he showed his work enough. That was my feeling. Having a secure job as an instructor in Queens College, dedicating his work to his immediate visual surroundings, my impression is, I don't know, that he didn't have many shows, and so that What I originally said about him being a loner means to me that from what I can judge, he also must have felt like an outsider. And so that when this big sweeping wave of abstract expressionists came along, I think he got kind of magnetized or pulled in by it and changed his style very much.
Do you think he would have been a different artist if he wasn't in Queens and if he wasn't so much of a loner?
I very definitely think so, because when I saw the show at the Queens Museum years later, what year was that?

1974. I was amazed to see some early canvases. And I went up to him to tell him, I think in the 20s, they were beautifully painted, and no one knew about them whatsoever. And the range of his work was rather remarkable. But I think he kept much to himself, although I'm sure his wife, who was practically his secretary, his helpmeet, his spokesperson, and so on, I think it was his own doing. I don't think he, maybe because he had a secure job, he didn't feel he had a show much, whatever it was. I feel that any poet, any composer, any artist, any writer has not a duty to society, but a duty to himself to show his work if he wants to have anyone understand or appreciate and so on. And I think he was very remiss on that angle(?). And maybe his wife tried to tell him. Maybe he didn't have the gumption to go around the galleries. Or maybe he had a few different... I have no faintest idea. In fact, I don't know how he got a show at the Mint Museum. I can understand how he had a show at the Queen's Museum because he was a Queen's resident and he had painted the Queen's scenes all his life. Can you describe for me how Sievan's style changed from the 30s to the 40s, the 50s, the 60s? Do you have that?

No, when he called me to see his work, the first large body work I saw was just before that Mint Museum. Now that was work of the 40s and maybe the 50s, and I wrote about it as best as I could and I'm sure you can quote anything you want out of that. But after that, it was in the mid-60s, mid and late 60s that it began to change, I think. That was a period of his change and I expressed my disappointment although he did it with a lot of panache. I was disappointed in the fact that he didn't incorporate much of his wonderful early work. Okay. Let's go.
Roll tape again. On tape.
Okay. We're rolling?
Yep. Rolling in speed.

Okay. Now, during the late 50s, from, I guess, around, after the Mint Museum, from 55 through maybe 57, Maurice had a whole series of conceptual paintings. I don't know if you're aware of this, but did he ever discuss this? No.
Conceptual paintings? No. What do you mean by conceptual paintings? Well, he was kind of reading a lot of philosophy and metaphysics and things like that. He was always into that, yeah.
Can you talk about that a little bit?

Well, I gather that because he could quote from a philosopher or from the Bible quite easily, always in a kind of mystical sardonic tone. And I didn't go into great lengths in those conversations, but I would hear a few sentences if I asked him some questions about that. I really haven't got a deep knowledge of that, but there was feelings of that, that he was getting almost like a man going into the Kabbalah or something. I don't know. That's a feeling I had. And maybe that was due to the living out and flushing by himself so much with his wife and not having so much contact, social contact, daily or weekly like most of us artists in the city. You know, we're all city rats and we bump into each other, groceries, exhibitions here and there,

meetings and so on, you know what I mean? And I think he was out of that. And I'm not sure that that helped him particularly. Sometimes, I'm not trying to use the word parochial, provincial, but sometimes a man gets to be, a man or woman, gets to be too withdrawn and gets into books and philosophy and so on as a redeeming quality, and that makes them even more isolated.
Okay. Can you tell me, just for background information, what was the WPA, and also how did Maurice Sievan fit in with the WPA artist?

Well, I never knew he was on the WPA, but the WPA was formed around 1934-5 in the famous New Deal projects that George Biddle talked Franklin Delano Roosevelt, our president, because they were both college chums, into the fact that Biddle was a painter, talked him into having art projects. or Harry Hopkins, or whoever he talked into, and they did that. And the first thing was there had to be social mural paintings for hospitals, post offices, high schools, and so on. But it branched out into murals, then easel paintings. We fought to have a project just so we could do our own creative painting. And then there was teaching. And then there was the American Index of Design. That was the four categories. American Index of Design was preserving early American designs, whether it was patchwork quilts, old jugs, and whatever, furniture and so on. And they did marvelous copies. And there's been two books published on the objects, early American objects, that the artists faithfully and beautifully copied from early American art. Oh, there was a fifth project that was graphic work, where people did etchings, lithographs, and silkscreen. Due to the WPA, that silkscreen was developed and invented. First it was commercial, then they developed it, so it became an art form, and it became very widely used, Even Rauschenberg uses it to this day, and so do a lot of contemporary artists, and it was developed, really, during the WPA. Now, I didn't know that he was on a project, but maybe did he teach or do easel paintings? Do you know what he did?
No, I don't know exactly what his WPA projects were.

Maybe he taught art or maybe he did easel paintings out in Flushing and brought them in once every month to the project. I don't know. I didn't meet him in those days. Well, as a matter of fact, it's interesting that you mentioned the silk screen because Maurice was one of the first people, apparently, who had been involved in the silk screen process. Really?
And he even went over to the Soviet Union for a year or two years to teach the Soviets how to work. Is that so?
That's interesting.
I think that that might have been in the 20s, actually.
No, he couldn't have done silkscreens in the 20s.
I have it written down in my office.

Yeah. No, it's got to be the 30s. It's got to be the 30s. Now, he might have been on the graphic division, and the only one you could ask and call up about it, and I'll give you the number later, is Jacob Kainen, who was on that graphic division, and he would tell you if he was on it. Okay.
He's in Washington, D.C., yeah.
Great. Now, you wrote an introduction to the Sievan exhibit at the Mint Museum. Can you recall the show? Did you go down to the show?

No. I saw the paintings he was going to show at the museum. He brought out 25 or 30 paintings, and I was absolutely intrigued with them, and I thought they were wonderful. And I was very happy to write. I never write. I never praise anybody dishonestly. It's against my principles. But I was terribly fond of the work, and I think I wrote a fairly warm tribute to the work. in that show. As a matter of fact, Maurice, although I almost demurred, insisted on giving me a small painting of that period for doing the review and write-up of the show. He liked it so much and naturally he could twist my arm and I accepted because I liked his work. Right. Now, later on, There was a whole New York School of Artists. Was Maurice Sievan part of the New York School?

No, he was not. But living in Provincetown in the summertime, he knew some of them. He knew Rothko, and I think he knew Motherwell. I don't know who he knew there. He knew Mervin Jules. He knew, well, all the artists drank beer in the same places, you know what I mean. So he knew the whole gang there. But I think, as I told you before in one of your other questions, that he felt that with this abstract expressionist movement taking over in the American art world, and especially the New York art world, that he felt time was passing him by. And I don't think he joined it in an opportunistic sense at all. I think he felt that there was something to this. Since he was partly expressionist in his work anyway, he felt that their use of non-subject matter and expressing your innards, so to speak, with washes(?) , he felt was an extension of his own feeling, as I say, as an expressionist. Abstract expressionism simply means you don't use subject matter, but you try to express your own inner feelings as he did in his streets anyway. And thereupon, he began to do some figure portraits. he didn't leave subject matter alone entirely. He did some figure portraits that were so simplified that it would be one shape or one or two shapes on the canvas. So in other words, I think he was still true to himself, but I expressed my disappointment. That's only a personal judgment. Now, I know that Maurice had gotten together on the It. There was an 8th Street gatherings and things like that, and he had been getting together with, even though he was living in Queens, he was coming in and getting together with some of those artists and some of those gatherings, and apparently there were a fairly large group of people, not just the big names. Not just Pollock and Rothko, yeah, and Motherwell.
You happen to know of any of those times?

I never met him there. I'll tell you why. I felt I was very much... divorced from that movement, I was digging into, I was doing a series of studio interiors, which at that time, which you might say was expressing my inners, and the subject matter wasn't what you'd call like my street scenes or portraits I was doing. It was a series of windows, mullion windows in the studio with some objects in front of them, which was as near abstract as you could get, but I made many variations of them, and I felt that their obsessive use of just color and shapes were not enough for me. I felt it was too limited, and I went there a couple of times. One time they had a party from Marino Marini, the wonderful Italian sculptor, and I liked his work so much I went up there. We had drinks and punch and so on. And another time I went up for some symposium which I thought was so obfuscated. I didn't know what they were talking about. And they were very pretentious, especially Motherwell and some of the others. And so I didn't go to those meetings. They invited me very often because I knew them all from the 30s. But I felt was a little too pretentious, large canvases, not much subject matter, and they were blowing

themselves up to pretentious proportions. I didn't go for Pollock's work. I liked some of de Kooning's work, but later I got to like Mark Rothko's work because I thought the color schemes were very beautiful and i thought they were much better than his figurative stuff whereas i felt that Adolf Gottlieb when he went abstract didn't know what the hell abstraction was about and his figurative early work was much better but that's a subjective opinion so i did not meet Maurice at those meetings I only went to about two of them

Yeah, do you have any ideas i mean you said that you felt that uh you personally felt that a lot of those artists were very pretentious they probably were um do you have any idea of how Maurice might have felt about some of those artists at that time No, I don't but I as I told you earlier that when I met him around the late 60s and he told me how much he liked that new book that was put out on my art my art show he told me he'd been visiting Rothko a little before he committed suicide I can't remember it was before or afterwards and I was a little surprised to know that he had become a close friend or I shouldn't been surprised because Rothko lived in Provincetown in the summer also I don't know why I was a little surprised but I didn't know that they after all I was a friend of Rothko's for the five years that we had a group called The 10 that we used to show around town I didn't know, and I knew that Rothko and Sievan knew each other in the Federation before I joined. I joined rather late because I felt, though they said it was a non-political group, I thought they talked against the left so much that they were political. And so I didn't want to join them. But later on, when it was non-political, and I had many friends in the group, I did join them. I can't remember whether it was in the late 50s or whatever. But I don't remember seeing Rothko or Gottlieb there more than a couple of times. I guess I joined when they were almost ready to quit the group and go on their own.

Right. Actually, Maurice had rented Rothko's studio in Provincetown for three years in the late 50s. Yeah, well, I think Rothko went to Paris or something, and Maurice and Lee spent their summers and worked in his studio.
Oh, really?
That's where he did a lot of that.
No, so he obviously become a close friend of Rothko. I didn't know that until he told me so in the 60s.

Now, do you have any other anecdotes about Sievan's relationship with either Mark Rothko or Milton Avery? Because he was also very close with Milton Avery. Yeah, we all admired Avery. Avery we all admired from the 30s on, from the mid-30s on. And he was, to us, like Manet might have been to the Impressionists, you know. that Claude Monet and Pissarro and Degas looked up to Manet because he kind of broke the ground. The critics used to pan him, and he took the brunt of the attack, and they looked up to him for that reason. That's how Avery was with our group. But strangely enough, in my visits to Avery many times, and my wife, I never met Maurice there.
Do you have any anecdotes about Maurice or any firsthand knowledge or recollection of Maurice with either Rothko or Avery that you could share?

No. The only thing I told you about was when in the late, I think it was after the suicide of Rothko, he told me that he had gone to Rothko and he'd seen these black and gray canvases. And I said, "didn't you realize that he was very deeply depressed when such a beautiful colorist was just painting black and gray? Couldn't you have told him to go to an analyst or something?" He said, "I talked to him, but I didn't realize he was in such trouble" or something like that. That's all I can recall.
Okay. Now, as an artist, can you tell me about Maurice's technique and his technical abilities with paint and canvas?

Well, after seeing that show at the Queen's College, I can tell you that I was amazed at the variety of fine technical qualities he had in his work. Because I saw some work in the 30s. I forget whether they were landscapes or whatever. But they were so beautifully painted that I went up and maybe there were a few portraits. I think there were a couple of portraits there I was highly impressed with since I do an awful lot of portraits. I went up to tell him how beautiful they were, and then he, little by little, he went into that suburban Flushing street painting that I always liked so much, which was quite different. There he loosened up and had the paint strokes pell-mell come in and out, overlap and so forth. And he got a certain immediacy out of them. You almost felt that they were done at one sitting, that he had to get the impression right away. I don't think they were all one sitting, but some of them may have been three, four, five sittings. But some of them absolutely, like the one he gave me, looks to me like it was a one- sitting scrambled eggs thing, but it was beautiful in its way. So he had quite a variety of techniques. He was technically very resourceful, more than most painters are today.
Now, it seems as if Maurice Sievan didn't want to sell his work. That I never knew.

Okay, well, after 1965 with that museum show, he didn't even show his work very much. He had a couple gallery shows, and that was basically it for a long period of time. Do you know anything about this, or did he ever discuss..?

No, he never did. I never had the faintest idea that he didn't want to sell his work. When an artist has so many pictures around, and you told me that anecdote about that picture he wanted back, I find that incomprehensible except for the fact that Maurice was always a little strange and individualistic. And while it doesn't overwhelm me, it surprises me a little bit. Do you have any insights into Maurice's work specifically as he changed his style? No, I can only describe what I've seen. I really can't. I told you why what I think happened was that he felt his earlier work was a little too localized, parochial, and he felt that this movement was larger and more philosophical and so on. And I think he drifted to it. Do you think that Sievan deserves wider recognition?
Absolutely.
Can you make a statement out of that?

well, my feeling is that he went through three or four periods in his life, and there are some artists go through eight periods. And all the periods, I thought the early period when I saw the Queen's College with some of the portraits deserve to be seen, and I don't think anyone knows about them outside of those people. You know, a show like that, Adam, outside of the opening night when all his friends and many artists are there, how many people traipse into that museum to see the show? So I would say the world at large does not know his early work of the 20s. Only a partial part of the public knows his work of the 30s and 40s and 50s, and hardly anyone knows his late work at all. So I would say his work is, the word obscure isn't enough, His work is hidden. He's buried. And I certainly think it's wonderful that he had a nephew like

Howard to revive and try to revive his work. Because that show at the National Arts Club was a beautiful show. And I sent a few people to see it. But, you know, they don't gain much of an audience. because though they did send out a lot, they told me to send out a lot of catalogs or prospects and so on, whatever they could, I had to tell a few painters to see it. They didn't know a damn thing about it. And I only caught it by the gallery guide catalog, even though Howard was nice enough to advertise it in the Times. And you need a gallery, you need a gallery to love his work, as many of us do, and show it in a retrospective scale, examples of different periods, then a one-man show of one period, then a year or two later a show of another period of his with very good writings by critical figures like Hilton Kramer, Greenberg, or somebody else, or Ted Wolf, the Christian Science Monitor. And to rehabilitate Maurice Sievan's work, if you've got a good gallery to do it, would take at least five years. That's my estimate. Yeah, I think you're right, at least.
(Unintelligible) Okay.
Okay. So, yeah, let's talk about that. I just remembered it. I just remembered it. You say that was in the 70s?

yeah I remember he either called me up or invited me to see some new works of his and there were maybe no more than a half a dozen people there but I distinctly remember Roselle Davis since I knew her all the way from the 30s and he was showing us very small paperwork with black and some kind of configurations pretty abstract but they were wonderful little notes tiny little notes it looked like to me on four by six pieces of paper or something and he showed us a great number of them they were most very intriguing I remember that Roselle Davis, Stuart Davis's widow was fascinated with 'em and she read about it said They ought to be seen. But obviously, he didn't go around knocking at doors because, in fact, that's one of the most interesting phases of his work that I ever saw. And it just comes to mind now when you mention that phase of his work.
Let me tell you something about that work. He did them in Provincetown. He crumpled them up and threw them on the floor. And Lee would go and pick them up and mount them.

I believe that. I believe that. I believe that, yeah. Yeah, he had that, that's something strange he saw. Did he ever go to an analyst in his life? I don't know. He sure needed one. Can you recollect anything else with Stuart Davis' widow?
No, I remember that occasion.
Was there anything else at that occasion? Was that up at his apartment? Up at his apartment, yeah, up in New York.

And did she have any, you know, this is a little interesting to me since I just saw the Stuart Davis exhibit yesterday. Did she have anything to say about some of his other work? Was this the first time?

No. Well, I don't know what her connection was with him before that. He might have had, he must have known her because she didn't seem like a stranger there. And I hadn't seen her for some time. But all of us were raving about it. But I remember particularly she and I were saying they ought to be seen. You know, you've got to get a gallery to show this stuff. That's all I remember of it. And she was highly enthusiastic, and rightly so in my opinion, because I was too.

Great. Now, this is the last question I have written down. It's been 10 years since this death. And is there anything that you can say about Maurice Sievan and his work, his vision, that would kind of sum it up?

Well, I actually think I've, along the trail, I've given you enough. My feeling is that he certainly needs a rehabilitation. He's a perfectly fine artist, unusual artist, an original artist, and one that has quality, that is so superior to the haphazard work done today, the conceptual work, the installations, the dislocations, the photographic reproductions of work, the work of people who just do lettering and sayings on walls, and so on. I think the art world has reached a nadir, a low point, And certainly, Sievan was one of the individual, original adventurers of that period, of the 30s, 40s, 50s, and all the way to the 70s. And he has enough variety of his work. I don't recall those little drawings at the Queen's show. Were they there?
I don't think so.

I'll have to count out(?), which is a shame, because that would put a final imprint on the arc of his work, I feel that the right gallery could easily, over a period of time, rehabilitate him and make him commensurate with his real worth.
Right. Now, is there anything else that... I haven't touched on or I haven't asked you that you'd like to say or anything that you can think about?

Well, I think I've gone off the periphery of your questions, and I'm glad you brought up those late little sketches that he did in pieces of paper because I was very impressed with them, and I think I liked them more than the larger abstract expressionist works of his, And I think a show of them, maybe an initial show of them, because they would be closer to the current stream, with the right kind of write-up by Clement Greenberg or someone of stature like that, would kind of push him into a new prominence better than showing his early work. Then you'd go backwards, you know, like a movie that, what's the word when you do flashback? Flashback, you know, you'd start with that. I think would, you know, I'm going to tell Howard that. You'd start with that nice show, about 30 or 50 of those little sketches of his. Then flash back to his early work in the next show and on to his different periods. Would be a wonderful way, I think, if I were a gallery dealer, to present him.
that's great
